subject: chemistry

moments.title: Dalton's atomic theory
moments.body:
Dalton, a Quaker schoolteacher with no university post, presents a paper proposing that elements are made of indivisible atoms. Different elements have atoms of different mass. Compounds form by simple integer ratios of atoms.

He uses the law of multiple proportions (carbon and oxygen form CO with 1:1 mass ratio and CO2 with 1:2) as evidence.

quote.text: We might as well attempt to introduce a new planet into the solar system, or annihilate one already in existence, as to create or destroy a particle of hydrogen.

moments.takeaway: Dalton's atoms are indivisible billiard balls. This is the first quantitative atomic theory of modern science.

moments.title: Thomson discovers the electron
moments.who: J. J. Thomson, Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge
moments.body:
Cathode rays — glowing streams in evacuated tubes — were known but mysterious. Thomson shows they consist of negatively charged particles with charge-to-mass ratio about 1000 times that of hydrogen ions.

The particles are the same regardless of which gas is in the tube or which metal makes the cathode. Thomson proposes they are sub-atomic — pieces of all atoms.

quote.text: I have been driven to the conclusion that they are charges of negative electricity carried by particles of matter.

moments.takeaway: The atom is no longer the smallest thing. Dalton's billiard ball has internal structure.

moments.title: Rutherford's gold foil experiment
moments.body:
Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil. Most pass through, as expected from Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (positive charge spread out, with electrons embedded). But about 1 in 8000 bounce backwards.

Rutherford described his reaction: 'It was as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'

The data force a new model: positive charge is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus, with electrons orbiting at a distance.
moments.takeaway: The atom is mostly empty space. A dense nucleus, surrounded by electrons at huge relative distance.

moments.title: Bohr's quantised orbits
moments.body:
Classical electromagnetism predicts orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus. They don't. Hydrogen's emission spectrum has discrete lines, not a continuous spectrum.

Bohr proposes electrons orbit in 'quantised' orbits — only specific radii allowed, only specific energies. Jumping between orbits emits a photon of frequency f = (E1 - E2)/h.

The theory reproduces hydrogen's Rydberg formula exactly. It also has obvious flaws — it doesn't work for any other atom.
moments.takeaway: Quantisation is in. The classical picture of orbits is on borrowed time.

moments.title: Schrödinger's wave equation
moments.body:
Schrödinger writes down a wave equation governing the electron's wavefunction. Solving for hydrogen gives orbitals (s, p, d, f) — not classical orbits but probability distributions.

Heisenberg's matrix mechanics (1925) gives an equivalent picture. The Pauli exclusion principle (1925) explains why electrons fill shells. Quantum mechanics becomes the foundation of modern chemistry.

quote.text: I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it.
quote.attrib: Erwin Schrödinger, on the probabilistic interpretation of his own equation

moments.takeaway: Atoms are governed by wavefunctions, not orbits. Chemistry is quantum mechanics applied to electrons in fields of nuclei.

now.title: Atoms today
now.body:
The atom is made of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) and a cloud of electrons described by wavefunctions. Protons and neutrons are themselves made of quarks (up and down) bound by gluons. Quantum chromodynamics describes that level.

We can image individual atoms (scanning tunnelling microscope, 1981), trap single atoms in lasers, and manipulate them with optical tweezers (2018 Nobel).
now.open_questions: Is there a deeper structure inside quarks? The Standard Model has 17 fundamental particles — why these specifically? Why are there three families of matter? Why is the electron mass exactly what it is?

reflection: Dalton was colour-blind (the first scientific description of colour blindness, by Dalton himself). He never knew sodium emits yellow light because he couldn't see yellow. How does a researcher's perceptual world shape what they choose to investigate?
